prompt: A Kubernetes Secret holds a service account key in base64. Who can read the key?
hint: Is base64 a lock?

choices.text: Only the pod that mounts it, which holds the decryption key
choices.why: There is nothing to decrypt; base64 has no key.

choices.text: Anyone with read access to the Secret
choices.why: Right. base64 is an encoding, and one line reverses it.

choices.text: Nobody, because Kubernetes encrypts Secrets with the cluster's key
choices.why: Encryption at rest protects the disk, not someone allowed to get the Secret.

choices.text: Only Google, which issued the key
choices.why: Google keeps no copy of the private key; whoever holds the file has it.

prompt: A key made for a test three years ago is found in an old CI log. What does it still do?
hint: Does a user-managed key expire by itself?

choices.text: Nothing: keys expire after ninety days
choices.why: No expiry applies unless an organisation policy sets one.

choices.text: Only read access, since old keys are downgraded
choices.why: Nothing downgrades a key.

choices.text: Everything the service account is allowed, from anywhere
choices.why: Right. Until someone deletes it, it is the service account.

choices.text: It works only from inside the cluster that used it
choices.why: A key works from any computer.

prompt: base64 is an encoding, not ___.
hint: What would need a key to undo?

prompt: Which organisation policy stops anyone creating service account keys?
hint: It is named after what it disables.

choices.text: iam.workloadIdentityUser
choices.why: That is a role, the one section 03 grants.

choices.text: storage.objectViewer
choices.why: A role on Storage, unrelated to keys.

choices.text: iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: GKE_METADATA
choices.why: A node pool setting, not a policy.

prompt: Which of these are problems of a static key? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of leaking, ending and rotating.

choices.text: A copy leaks with no sign in the audit log
choices.why: Right; the leaked key looks like the service account.

choices.text: Rotating it means updating every Secret that holds it
choices.why: Right; which is why it gets put off.

choices.text: It stops working when the pod restarts
choices.why: It keeps working, which is the problem.

choices.text: It can only be used against Cloud Storage
choices.why: It acts as the service account against any API.

prompt: What is the workload pool of every cluster in the project planner-dev?
hint: One per project.

choices.text: shop.svc.id.goog, named after the cluster
choices.why: The pool is named after the project.

choices.text: planner-dev.svc.id.goog, shared by its clusters
choices.why: Right; shared by every cluster in the project with it on.

choices.text: planner-dev.iam.gserviceaccount.com
choices.why: That is the domain of Google service accounts' emails.

choices.text: A pool created per namespace
choices.why: Namespaces are inside the pool's names, not pools of their own.

prompt: Where is roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser granted in section 03?
hint: The binding lets an identity use something.

choices.text: On the bucket shop-photos
choices.why: The bucket gets storage.objectViewer.

choices.text: On the project, for all service accounts
choices.why: Granting it project-wide would let the pod act as any of them.

choices.text: On the Kubernetes service account, through its annotation
choices.why: The annotation names an email; IAM bindings live in Google, not in the cluster.

choices.text: On the Google service account photos-reader
choices.why: Right; it lets [shop/photos] act as that one account.

prompt: terraform validate refused member = "planner-dev.svc.id.goog[shop/photos]". What was missing?
hint: A member names its kind first.

choices.text: The serviceAccount: prefix before the name
choices.why: Right. Every member names its kind before the identity.

choices.text: The project number before the pool
choices.why: Only the principal:// form carries a number.

choices.text: Quotes around the brackets
choices.why: Brackets are part of the name and need no quoting.

choices.text: A namespace other than shop
choices.why: shop is right; the format was the problem.

prompt: A Kubernetes ServiceAccount names the Google identity it uses with the annotation iam.gke.io/gcp-service-___.
hint: The last word of the annotation's key.

prompt: On a Standard cluster, the node pool lacks workload_metadata_config GKE_METADATA, and everything else of section 03 is in place. What does the photos pod get when it asks for a token?
hint: Who answers 169.254.169.254 on that node?

choices.text: A token for photos-reader, because the binding exists
choices.why: The binding is never consulted; GKE's server is not in the path.

choices.text: An error, because no metadata server runs on the node
choices.why: The node's own metadata server answers.

choices.text: A token for the node's own service account
choices.why: Right. That is the leak GKE_METADATA closes.

choices.text: The key from the old Secret, if it still exists
choices.why: The metadata server knows nothing of Secrets.

prompt: How many resources did the plan of wi/main.tf add?
hint: Account, binding on the account, binding on the bucket.

prompt: Put the steps of the token exchange in order.
hint: The pod asks first, Storage is called last.
items: The client library asks 169.254.169.254 for a token
GKE's metadata server gets the Kubernetes service account's token
The Security Token Service returns a federated token
The IAM credentials API issues a token for photos-reader
The library calls Cloud Storage with it

prompt: A pod gets "iam.serviceAccounts.getAccessToken denied". Which step failed, and what is the usual cause?
hint: Which call asks for a token for photos-reader?

choices.text: Step 5: the bucket has no role for photos-reader
choices.why: That gives a 403 from Storage, after a token was issued.

choices.text: Step 2: the node pool lacks GKE_METADATA
choices.why: Then the pod would get the node's token, not this error.

choices.text: Step 4: the workloadIdentityUser binding is missing or misnamed
choices.why: Right; a typo in [shop/photos] is the usual one.

choices.text: Step 1: the container cannot reach the address 169.254.169.254 at all
choices.why: Then there would be no IAM error at all.

prompt: How long is the access token the pod receives valid for?
hint: Short-lived, and refreshed by the library.

choices.text: Until the pod is deleted
choices.why: Tokens expire on their own.

choices.text: Ninety days, like a rotated key
choices.why: Nothing in this exchange lasts days.

choices.text: About an hour
choices.why: Right; a stolen token stops working within the hour.

choices.text: As long as the node keeps running
choices.why: The node's life does not set the token's.

prompt: The Deployment runs in the namespace shops, and the binding names [shop/photos]. What happens, and why is it hard to spot?
hint: IAM compares names exactly.

choices.text: IAM matches shop to shops and grants the token
choices.why: Names are compared exactly; there is no fuzzy match.

choices.text: Step 4 is denied, and IAM sees two identities without complaint
choices.why: Right. Nothing is invalid; it simply names somebody else.

choices.text: terraform validate refuses the binding because it looks like a typo
choices.why: The member is well formed; validate cannot know the namespace.

choices.text: The pod falls back to the node's service account
choices.why: With GKE_METADATA there is no fallback to the node.

prompt: The pod reaches the metadata server with the header Metadata-Flavor: ___.
hint: The same as on Compute Engine.

prompt: What does the principal:// identifier in a direct grant carry that serviceAccount: members do not?
hint: Twelve digits.

choices.text: The project number
choices.why: Right; not the id, the number Google assigns.

choices.text: The Google service account's email
choices.why: A direct grant has no Google service account.

choices.text: The cluster's name
choices.why: The pool is per project; no cluster is named.

choices.text: An expiry date for the grant
choices.why: Grants carry no expiry here.

prompt: Why is project_number a variable set to twelve zeros in wi/direct.tf?
hint: Does planner-dev exist at Google?

choices.text: Zeros mean "this project" to IAM
choices.why: IAM gives zeros no special meaning.

choices.text: The provider fills in the real number at plan time from Google
choices.why: Nothing reaches Google to ask.

choices.text: This lab's planner-dev has none to give; it is a stand-in
choices.why: Right. On a real project the variable gets the real number.

choices.text: Project numbers are secret and must not be written down
choices.why: A project number is an identifier, not a secret.

prompt: The shop's nightly job on a virtual machine must read shop-photos as the same identity as the pod. Which arrangement fits?
hint: Which identity exists outside the cluster?

choices.text: A direct grant to principal://.../ns/shop/sa/photos for both
choices.why: That principal exists only inside the cluster's pool.

choices.text: A key file for the virtual machine, kept beside the job
choices.why: That brings back the problem of section 01.

choices.text: The service-account way: both act as photos-reader
choices.why: Right. One named Google service account, one place to grant and revoke.

choices.text: Two direct grants with different project numbers
choices.why: The virtual machine is not a Kubernetes identity at all.

prompt: Which of these does the direct grant remove, compared with section 03? Choose all that apply.
hint: One identity, one binding.

choices.text: The Google service account photos-reader
choices.why: Right; there is nothing to impersonate.

choices.text: The workloadIdentityUser binding
choices.why: Right; nothing is acted as.

choices.text: The workload pool planner-dev.svc.id.goog
choices.why: The principal is named inside that pool.

choices.text: The role on the bucket
choices.why: Some role on the bucket is the whole point.

prompt: A service account's account_id must have between 6 and how many characters?
hint: The provider's refusal said it.

prompt: Match each symptom to the step of the exchange that failed.
hint: Section 04's table.

pairs.left: A token for the node's service account

pairs.right: Step 5, no role on the bucket

prompt: After moving to Workload Identity, what should happen to the old photos-key Secret and its key?
hint: A key keeps working until somebody deletes it.

choices.text: Keep them as a fallback in case the exchange fails
choices.why: A fallback key is the leak you set out to remove.

choices.text: Delete the Secret; the key expires by itself later
choices.why: The key does not expire on its own.

choices.text: Nothing: Workload Identity disables keys automatically
choices.why: Nothing disables an existing key for you.

choices.text: Delete the key at Google and the Secret in the cluster
choices.why: Right. Until the key is deleted, every copy still works.

prompt: A workload pool is always the project id followed by .svc.id.___.
hint: Four letters, Google's own.
